additions.title: UK GDPR, Article 28: Processor
additions.quote: allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections, conducted by the controller or another auditor mandated by the controller
additions.why: The one audit right that general UK law writes into supplier contracts. Where a supplier processes personal data on the buyer's behalf, the contract must require it to make available the information needed to show compliance and to allow audits and inspections by the buyer or its auditor. Applies only where personal data is processed and the supplier is a processor, so it does not reach every AI purchase. Current revised text on legislation.gov.uk.

additions.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 8.1: General outsourcing requirements
additions.locator: SYSC 8.1.8R(9); also 8.1.6R (firm remains fully responsible), 8.1.7R (due skill, care and diligence), 8.1.8R(2), (6), (7) and (12) (performance review, disclosure of material developments, termination, continuity). Provisions shown as dated 23/10/2025
additions.quote: must have effective access to data related to the outsourced activities, as well as to the business premises of the service provider
additions.why: A binding regulator rule, not guidance. A firm that outsources critical or important functions must assess the supplier's performance on an ongoing basis, be told of material developments, be able to terminate, keep continuity on exit, and have access for itself and its auditors to the supplier's data and premises. Sector-specific: these rules bind 'common platform firms' as the Handbook defines them, and SYSC 8.1.1AG tells other firms to treat the main outsourcing rule as guidance; it covers outsourcing of critical or important functions, not every purchase. Not written for AI.

additions.title: AI Act, Article 25: Responsibilities along the AI value chain (AI Act Service Desk copy)
additions.locator: Article 25(4), marked AMENDED; 'About this text' notice
additions.quote: shall, by written agreement, specify the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance based on the generally acknowledged state of the art
additions.why: The Commission's own copy, not the Official Journal; it says the text follows the EUR-Lex consolidated version of the AI Act as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes. The provider of a high-risk system and any third party supplying a model, tool, component or service built into it must set out in a written agreement the information and technical access the provider needs to comply. A duty between provider and upstream supplier, not on a deployer; relevant only to organisations within the Act's reach, and the high-risk rules are not yet in application.

additions.title: AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes report
additions.locator: Executive summary, pp.3-4; 'Third party relationships' section, p.47 onwards (recommendations for recruiters)
additions.quote: Some had attempted to pass all responsibility for compliance to recruiters using their tool.
additions.why: A regulator's audit finding on what suppliers actually do. In consensual audits of AI recruitment tool providers the regulator found providers wrongly calling themselves processors, vague contracts that left the buying recruiter 'in the dark', and attempts to pass all responsibility to the buyer. It recommends that buyers obtain evidence of controls before purchase and run compliance checks through the life of the contract. Recruitment tools only; data protection only; the number of organisations audited is small.

additions.title: Government's approach to technology suppliers: addressing the challenges (HC 543, Session 2024-25)
additions.locator: Summary, key finding citing paragraphs 2.8, 2.11, 2.13 and 2.15 (p.9); paragraphs 2.13-2.15 ('Being an intelligent client')
additions.quote: departments dedicate substantial resources to putting a contract in place but insufficient attention and resources to managing the contract after award
additions.why: The public auditor's finding on through-life supplier management: effort goes into letting a technology contract and too little into managing it afterwards, and government 'struggles to act as an intelligent client'. Estimates at least £14 billion a year of government digital procurement. About digital and technology suppliers in central government generally; AI is mentioned only as part of a market dominated by very large suppliers. Not a study of AI procurement.

additions.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
additions.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), published by The National Archives
additions.locator: Paragraph 199 (Ground 5, public sector equality duty); paragraphs 200-201
additions.quote: for reasons of commercial confidentiality, the manufacturer is not prepared to divulge the details so that it could be tested
additions.why: A court finding on buying AI without checking it. The police force had never satisfied itself, directly or through independent verification, that bought-in facial recognition software was free of unacceptable race or sex bias; the supplier would not release details of its training data. The court held that a supplier's commercial confidentiality does not let a public authority discharge its own non-delegable equality duty. Binding on public authorities under the Equality Act 2010 section 149; it is not a ruling about private-sector buyers.

additions.title: Understanding accountability in algorithmic supply chains
additions.publisher: Jennifer Cobbe, Michael Veale and Jatinder Singh (arXiv; ACM FAccT 2023)
additions.quote: challenges for allocating accountability stemming from distributed responsibility for systems between actors, limited visibility due to the accountability horizon
additions.why: Peer-reviewed conference paper, read on the authors' arXiv copy. Argues that AI is increasingly delivered through chains of suppliers linked by data flows, and that this spreads responsibility between actors and limits how far any one of them, the deploying organisation included, can see along the chain. Conceptual and legal analysis, not an empirical study; it explains why a buyer's due diligence cannot stop at the immediate vendor.

additions.title: Dislocated Accountabilities in the AI Supply Chain: Modularity and Developers' Notions of Responsibility
additions.publisher: David Gray Widder and Dawn Nafus (arXiv; Big Data & Society 10(1), 2023)
additions.quote: our participants often did not see the questions posed in responsible artificial intelligence guidelines to be within their agency, capability, or responsibility to address
additions.why: Empirical evidence from the supplier side. In interviews with 27 AI engineers, participants commonly treated questions of harm as the job of the previous or next party in the supply chain. Shows why a buyer cannot assume the vendor has done the checking. Small qualitative sample; where the engineers worked is not stated in the abstract. Read on the authors' arXiv copy of a journal article.

additions.title: Buying AI: Is the public sector equipped to procure technology in the public interest?
additions.locator: Executive summary ('A review of guidance, legislation and policy documents'); 'Document analysis'
additions.quote: local government does not have access to a clear or comprehensive account of how to procure AI in the public interest
additions.why: A UK documentary review of 16 pieces of guidance, legislation and policy on procuring AI and data-driven systems. Finds the guidance fragmented and leaves local authorities to interpret fairness, transparency and supplier responsibilities for themselves. An independent research institute's report, not peer reviewed; the documents reviewed were all published under the 2010-24 government, so the 2025 AI Playbook and the Procurement Act's commencement post-date it.

additions.title: Updated EU AI model contractual clauses (MCC-AI)
additions.locator: Description; file list (commentary, high-risk version, light version)
additions.quote: a full version for high-risk AI, aligned with the EU AI Act adopted on 13 June 2024
additions.why: Ready-made contract terms for buying AI: a full set for high-risk systems, a lighter set for other AI, and a commentary on how to use them. Published by a community of practice of public buyers hosted by the Commission; voluntary, and drafted for EU law and public procurement. Only the landing page was read in this pass, not the clauses themselves. Useful as a starting point for the documentation, audit and change-notification terms the criterion's top level asks for.

rejected.reason: Not re-tried: iso.org returned HTTP 403 on 2 October and again today for another standard page. Paid standard; no free statement of the supplier clause could be read.

rejected.title: Procurement Act 2023, section 71
rejected.reason: Already referred to within the existing section 52 entry; adding it separately would pad the list.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the brief. One refinement: the sentence 'Elsewhere, beyond data protection duties, the expectations are guidance' follows the PRA and Procurement Act examples; FCA rule SYSC 8.1 is a further binding rule (access, termination and continuity for outsourced critical functions) for FCA common platform firms, and Bridges (2020) shows the public sector equality duty cannot be delegated to a supplier.
